clue.text: Bishop of London? No!

parts.note: a word meaning 'of London' (of the capital city) also names an archbishop who heads a province; London's bishop is not one, hence the 'No!'

explanation.surface: Someone guesses which prelate is meant and is firmly told they are wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: The word means both 'belonging to the capital' and 'an archbishop with authority over a province'. The Bishop of London is of the capital, yet he is no archbishop: in England only Canterbury and York hold that rank.
explanation.definitionFit: The term describes a senior churchman ruling a province of bishops, and also anything belonging to a capital city such as London.

clue.text: Highly-placed official with faithful audience

parts.note: a man who calls Muslims to prayer from high up in a minaret, his listeners being the faithful

explanation.surface: A senior functionary enjoys a loyal following.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Highly-placed' suggests seniority but means physically high, on a minaret; 'the faithful' are the believers called to prayer.
explanation.definitionFit: The crier who calls worshippers to prayer from a mosque tower stands high and is heard by believers.

clue.text: Trouble afoot for this holidaymaker?

parts.note: trouble with the feet is stumbling

explanation.surface: Something bad is brewing for a tourist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trouble afoot' means trouble brewing, but read literally it is a stumble, a trip, and a holiday outing is also a trip.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone on a short pleasure outing, especially a day excursion, is called this; it also means one who stumbles.

clue.text: Avoided being tackled in such a casual way

definitions.text: Avoided being tackled in such a casual way

parts.words: Avoided being tackled in such a casual way
parts.note: in rugby a player pushes off a tackler with the hand; done thus, the move is 'handed off', and the word means casual

explanation.surface: A player slipped a tackle almost lazily.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'hand-off' in rugby is fending off a tackler with an outstretched arm; reversing the phrase gives a word for brusque or casual.
explanation.definitionFit: Brusque and nonchalant, done without care or thought, as a casually dismissive remark.

clue.text: Perjurer named a very gallant gentleman

explanation.surface: A liar under oath is praised as a brave gentleman.
explanation.walkthrough: Titus Oates invented the 'Popish Plot' of 1678; Captain Lawrence Oates, who walked out to die on Scott's Antarctic expedition, is commemorated as 'a very gallant gentleman'.
explanation.definitionFit: Titus, the 17th-century fabricator of a Catholic plot, lied under oath; Captain Lawrence of Scott's polar party is memorialised for heroic sacrifice.

clue.text: President to prohibit a Japanese floral arrangement

parts.note: Ike was the nickname of President Eisenhower
to ban is to prohibit

explanation.surface: A US president moves to outlaw a Japanese flower display.
explanation.walkthrough: Ike is Dwight Eisenhower, US president 1953-61.
explanation.definitionFit: The Japanese art of arranging flowers in formal compositions.

clue.text: Folk-song about former kingdom

indicators.note: about means going round, so the song wraps around the folk

parts.note: an aria is a song in an opera
folk can mean people, men

explanation.surface: A traditional ballad concerns a vanished realm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Folk-song' looks like one thing; split it into 'Folk' (MEN) and 'song' (ARIA).
explanation.definitionFit: This Caucasus land was an ancient kingdom, the first to adopt Christianity as a state religion.

clue.text: I don't know how you can repose

explanation.surface: Someone shrugs at a question about how to relax.
explanation.walkthrough: 'repose' looks like rest but is re-pose: pose a question again.
explanation.definitionFit: A stock reply when stumped by a question; it is also a request to pose a fresh question, so re-pose.

clue.text: County appointment for North African tribeswoman

explanation.surface: A woman from a North African tribe is given an official post in an English county.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is a joke: the Riff (or Rif) are a Berber people of Morocco, so a woman of the tribe is a 'she-Riff'.
explanation.definitionFit: The crown's officer in a county holds this post; split as a female pronoun plus Riff, it is jokingly a woman of that Moroccan Berber people.

clue.text: The right moment's here for Dewar's invention

parts.note: a mo is a moment, and the 's adds an S

explanation.surface: Someone announces that the right moment has come for a Scotch whisky.
explanation.walkthrough: Dewar suggests the whisky maker, but this is Sir James Dewar, the scientist who invented the vacuum flask in 1892.
explanation.definitionFit: The scientist James Dewar devised the vacuum flask, which keeps drinks hot or cold and is widely known by this trade name.

clue.text: Spot earth's revolution — about ten miles up in this perhaps

definitions.text: ten miles up in this perhaps

indicators.note: a revolution turns things round, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: Someone spots the earth turning while about ten miles up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolution' shuffles SPOTEARTHS into STRATOSPHE; 'about' looks like 'approximately' but gives RE.
explanation.definitionFit: This atmospheric layer begins roughly ten miles above the ground, so a high-flying aircraft might be there.

clue.text: Confuse pages after opening Byron's poem

parts.note: to maze is an old word for bewilder or confuse

indicators.note: the opening of the word after is its first letter

explanation.surface: Someone jumbles the pages after the start of a poem by Byron.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after' looks like an instruction to place pieces, but 'opening' takes just its first letter, A.
explanation.definitionFit: Byron wrote a narrative poem of 1819 about a Ukrainian hetman tied to a wild horse, titled with his name.

clue.text: A useful tool one comes across

explanation.surface: A handy implement is something you happen to come across.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense reads 'one' as 'something that': a thing that spans or bridges a gap.
explanation.definitionFit: A wrench for turning nuts is a useful tool; read literally, the word is also something that spans or stretches over a gap.

clue.text: Israel's army captain gets a battalion to about-turn

parts.note: BN is the military abbreviation for battalion

indicators.note: turn tells us the word re, from about, is turned round to face the other way

parts.note: re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: An Israeli army officer orders a battalion to do an about-turn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about-turn' looks like a single drill command; split it: 'about' gives RE and 'turn' reverses it to ER.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Bible, Saul's cousin commanded the army of Israel as its captain.

clue.text: Legal speaker produces depression about girl

indicators.note: about means going round, so the depression wraps around the girl

parts.note: a dent is a small hollow or depression
Clara is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A lawyer's speech brings on gloom concerning a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'depression' suggests low spirits, but it is a physical hollow, DENT.
explanation.definitionFit: In law, a person who makes a formal statement or declaration is so called, so a legal speaker.

clue.text: Garnett, say, as boss gives one a pain in the neck

definitions.text: Garnett, say, as boss gives one a pain in the neck

parts.words: Garnett, say, as boss gives one a pain in the neck
parts.note: a red garnet gem cut as a rounded boss shares its name with a painful boil, often on the neck

explanation.surface: A domineering manager called Garnett is a real nuisance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boss' suggests a manager but means a rounded knob: a garnet cut smooth and rounded bears the same name as a boil.
explanation.definitionFit: A smooth rounded red gemstone and an abscess on the skin share this name, so it is both jewel and pain.

clue.text: Go in first for widespread military set-up

explanation.surface: Someone opens the batting for a broadly spaced army formation.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket to 'open' is to go in first in the batting order, so the opener goes in first in the order; the military sense is troops drawn up with wide spaces between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Read as a cricket instruction, open the batting line-up; as a drill term, a formation with gaps between soldiers.

clue.text: The cost of swans in the river

indicators.note: in places the swans inside the river

parts.note: the Exe is a river in Devon
pens are female swans

explanation.surface: Someone asks what keeping swans on the river costs.
explanation.walkthrough: The River Exe flows through Exeter in Devon, south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Expenditure, the amount something costs.

clue.text: A month on a Roman road builds up Antony's wife

indicators.note: in a down clue on means placed above, so this goes on top

parts.note: Oct is the abbreviation for October
via is Latin for road

explanation.surface: A month spent on a Roman road strengthens Antony's wife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'builds up' joins the pieces, written upwards in a down clue. Octavia, sister of Octavian, was Mark Antony's wife.
explanation.definitionFit: Mark Antony married Octavian's sister, who became his wife before he left her for Cleopatra.

clue.text: Islands in company with another

parts.note: with another company we have two of them, abbreviated Cos

explanation.surface: Some islands keep company with another group.
explanation.walkthrough: The group is the Cocos (Keeling) Islands in the Indian Ocean, an Australian territory.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cocos Islands are a small Australian-governed atoll group in the Indian Ocean.

clue.text: Gather this is how to save money on US calls

definitions.text: this is how to save money on US calls

explanation.surface: Someone learns how to cut the phone bill when calling in America.
explanation.walkthrough: In the US, calling 'collect' means reversing the charges, so the person called pays.
explanation.definitionFit: To gather is to assemble; a reverse-charge phone call in America is a call made this way.

clue.text: Flute selected by TV viewer

explanation.surface: A flute recital is picked by someone watching television.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flute' is not the instrument but a groove, as in a fluted column.
explanation.definitionFit: A groove cut in a column is a flute; television watchers pick a station by this.

clue.text: The cap I ordered for livery?

indicators.note: ordered means put into a fresh order, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone orders a peaked cap as part of a servant's uniform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'livery' looks like a servant's uniform, which the cap suits; read it as 'liver-y', to do with the liver.
explanation.definitionFit: This medical adjective means relating to the liver, which is what 'livery' jokingly says.

clue.text: Trace breakdown, ' showing something's missing

indicators.note: a breakdown breaks the word apart, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Analysing a trace reveals that something is absent.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition describes the proofreader's mark inserted where a word or letter has been left out.
explanation.definitionFit: The proofreading mark placed in text marks the place of an omission.

clue.text: Free French articles as hard to get

parts.note: un is a French indefinite article
le is a French definite article
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: French items can be had free of charge, but are hard to obtain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Free' is a verb here, to let loose.
explanation.definitionFit: To let loose a dog or a force is to set it free.

clue.text: Knocked down on reaching crease?

parts.note: in cricket a batter scores a run by reaching the crease at the other end
over can mean on, on top of

explanation.surface: A cricketer is bowled over just as they reach the crease.
explanation.walkthrough: The crease is the line at each end of a cricket pitch; running between them scores a run.
explanation.definitionFit: Hit by a vehicle and flattened, as a pedestrian struck by a car.

clue.text: One of those fraud victim's taken to daily

definitions.text: One of those fraud victim's taken to

explanation.surface: A swindled person goes off to work as a domestic help.
explanation.walkthrough: To be 'taken to the cleaners' is to be swindled; in Britain a 'daily' is a cleaning lady who comes in each day.
explanation.definitionFit: Being swindled is being taken to the cleaners, so one shop of that kind; a daily is a household help who tidies up.

clue.text: Go crazy, like Kipling's ditties

parts.note: to depart is to go away
mental is slang for crazy

explanation.surface: Kipling's light verses send a reader mad.
explanation.walkthrough: Kipling's first verse collection (1886) was 'Departmental Ditties', about Anglo-Indian officials.
explanation.definitionFit: Kipling's early verse book is titled 'Departmental Ditties', so the adjective describes those poems.
